extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of mathematics learning problem-solving heuristics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and heuristics for solving mathematical problems (both 'problems to prove' and 'problems to find'), including how to analyze statements, seek analogies, introduce auxiliary elements, carry out and check solutions, and teach/motivate steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the hypothesis and the conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask explicitly: 'What is the hypothesis?' and 'What is the conclusion?'. For problems to prove isolate hypothesis and conclusion; for problems to find identify unknown, data and conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly models questioning the student: 'What is the hypothesis?' 'What is the conclusion?' and recommends isolating principal parts. (See: 'The hypothesis and the conclusion are the principal parts of a “problem to prove”; the unknown, the data, and the conditions are the principal parts of a “problem to find.”')

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw a figure and introduce suitable notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw an appropriate diagram and choose convenient labels/notation before proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: student draws lines and chooses letters as in Fig. 4; in rate problem introduce V(t), y(t), x etc. The author emphasizes introducing geometric elements (center, radius) into the figure rather than stating them abstractly ('stating the definition without drawing something is mere lip-service').

rubrics_metrics.name: Work symbolically first; postpone numerical substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Disregard numerical values provisionally; work with letters/parameters and substitute numbers only after deriving the expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the conical vessel problem the teacher suggests 'disregard, provisionally, the numerical-values, work with the letters, express the unknown in terms of a, b, r, y and only finally ... substitute the numerical values.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolate and consider principal parts one by one and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Go through principal parts (hypothesis/conclusion or unknown/data/conditions), consider them one by one and in various combinations, relating details to the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From 'Working for Better Understanding': 'Go through the principal parts of your problem, consider them one by one, consider them in turn, consider them in various combinations, relating each detail to other details and each to the whole of the problem.' This prepares and clarifies details likely to play a role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek familiar theorems and analogous known results
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for previously proved theorems or familiar results that have the same or similar conclusion and consider whether they can be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialog example: student recalls 'If two triangles are congruent, the corresponding angles are equal' and the teacher prompts using such theorems. The text repeatedly advises 'try to think of a familiar theorem having the same or a similar conclusion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce auxiliary elements with purpose (auxiliary lines, unknowns, auxiliary problems/theorems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Add new elements to the figure or new auxiliary unknowns/theorems only when they serve to make use of known results or clarify the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition: 'An element that we introduce in the hope that it will further the solution is called an auxiliary element.' Examples include auxiliary lines in geometry, auxiliary unknowns in algebra, auxiliary theorems. Warning: 'We should not introduce auxiliary elements wantonly.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate and explain auxiliary steps to learners
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting or teaching solutions, give the motive and purpose for conspicuous auxiliary steps so intelligent readers are not left feeling cheated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers/authors are advised: 'If a tricky auxiliary line appears abruptly ... intelligent students and readers are disappointed; they feel that they are cheated.' Spend time making such steps comprehensible by remarks or carefully chosen questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy: consider simpler analogous problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for simpler analogous problems whose method or result can be used for the original problem (use method, result, or both).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections on analogy: solve the triangle before the tetrahedron; 'we may use the method of the simpler analogous problem or its result.' The text advises using simpler analogous cases as stepping stones and discusses inference by analogy and its strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the problem from various sides and seek contacts with prior knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine different parts, emphasize different details, recombine them differently, and try to recall what helped in similar situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From 'Hunting for the Helpful Idea': 'Consider your problem from various sides ... Seek contacts with your formerly acquired knowledge.' This increases chance of finding a helpful idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat incomplete or hazy ideas seriously and examine their potential
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have an incomplete idea, consider it further; ascertain how far it leads and reconsider the situation—it may lead to another idea or be refined into a usable plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'If it looks advantageous you should consider it longer. If it looks reliable you should ascertain how far it leads you, and reconsider the situation.' Be grateful even for hazy or supplementary ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stepping-stone connections when direct connection is unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: If you cannot see the direct connection between given quantities and the unknown, try to bring in a simpler connection that could serve as a stepping stone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the rate problem: 'If you do not see yet the connection between [derivative] and the data, try to bring in some simpler connection that could serve as a stepping stone.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce suitable intermediate variables and relations (express dependencies)
rubrics_metrics.description: When quantities depend on each other, introduce intermediate variables and seek relations (e.g., similar triangles give x:y = a:b) so you can express the unknown in terms of chosen parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate problem: introduce x as radius of free surface, note x and y are related by similar triangles x:y = a:b, then express V in terms of y and x, differentiate, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry out the plan with secure grasp and stepwise checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an idea is chosen, make your grasp secure and carry through algebraic or geometric operations in detail; convince yourself of correctness of each step by formal reasoning or intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From 'Carrying Out the Plan': 'If your problem is very complex distinguish 'great' steps and 'small' steps, check first the great steps, and get down to the smaller ones afterwards.' Aim for each step correct beyond doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish great steps from small steps when executing complex solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose complex solutions into major and minor steps; verify major steps first, then handle smaller details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit recommendation in 'Carrying Out the Plan' to distinguish 'great' steps composed of several small ones; check great steps first to ensure overall correctness before filling in details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Looking back: review, simplify, generalize and seek improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: After obtaining a complete solution, consider it from various sides, simplify and shorten parts, survey the whole at a glance, improve intuitiveness, scrutinize the method and result for reuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From 'Looking Back': 'Try to modify to their advantage smaller or larger parts of the solution, try to improve the whole solution, to make it intuitive, to fit it into your formerly acquired knowledge as naturally as possible.' Benefits include discovering new solutions or facts and developing problem-solving ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogical inference carefully but valuably
rubrics_metrics.description: Form plausible conjectures by analogy (e.g., centers of gravity for rod, triangle, tetrahedron); analogical conclusions from many clear parallel cases are stronger, but treat them as plausible not certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections discuss inference by analogy: 'Analogy is used on very different levels ... Inference by analogy appears to be the most common kind of conclusion ... It yields more or less plausible conjectures which may or may not be confirmed by experience and stricter reasoning.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clear-cut analogies and systematically arranged instances
rubrics_metrics.description: When strengthening a conjecture by analogy, favor clear, precise analogies and comparisons across several parallel cases rather than vague similarities or random cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'An analogical conclusion from many parallel cases is stronger ... Clear-cut analogies weigh more heavily than vague similarities, systematically arranged instances count for more than random collections of cases.' Example: segment→triangle→tetrahedron analogy strengthened by multiple comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose auxiliary problems whose profit (method or result) is clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Select auxiliary problems with an anticipated kind of profit: using their result, or learning a method that can be applied to the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: algebraic substitution leading to quadratic (x^4 -> y^2 - 13y + 36); plane problem used as auxiliary for solid geometry problem. 'The profit ... may be of various kinds: we may use the result of the auxiliary problem ... or its method.'

rubrics_metrics.name: When constructing, preserve natural symmetry of the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Place introduced elements (e.g., representation of perimeter p) so they respect problem symmetries (e.g., treat interchangeable sides equally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction example: earlier attempts placed p in ways that spoiled symmetry with respect to sides b and c; better placement preserves symmetry and suggests useful auxiliary lines (Fig. 11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid introducing auxiliary elements without reason; have some justification
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be some reason for introducing an auxiliary element; don't add elements wantonly just to complicate the figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit admonition: 'We may have this or that reason for introducing an auxiliary element, but we should have some reason. We should not introduce auxiliary elements wantonly.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Make definitions concrete by introducing the defining elements into the figure
rubrics_metrics.description: When invoking definitions (e.g., circle center and radius), draw and introduce those geometric elements into the figure to enable concrete use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From discussion: 'Going back to definitions, we have another opportunity to introduce auxiliary elements. Without introducing them, we could not make any concrete use of the definition; stating the definition without drawing something is mere lip-service.'
